title: Use completed-square form to identify a turning point

source_reference.notes: Original Edexcel 4MA1 Higher-style item for the Year 10 quadratics MVP. Edexcel pivot metadata applied.

problem_text: The function is y = x^2 - 6x + 8. Write it in completed-square form and state the coordinates of the turning point.
student_prompt: Show the completed-square form, then give the turning point.

error_category_mapping.diagnostic_sentence: In y = (x - 3)^2 - 1, the turning point is (3, -1). The x-coordinate has the opposite sign from the bracket.
(x - 3)^2 gives x^2 - 6x + 9, so the outside value must be -1 to make +8.

hint_ladder.title: What information does completed-square form give?
hint_ladder.prompt: Completed-square form lets you read the turning point of a quadratic graph. Think about the bracket value that makes the square smallest.

hint_ladder.title: Pick a starting move
hint_ladder.prompt: First rewrite the expression in completed-square form, then read the coordinates from that structure.

hint_ladder.title: A common slip
hint_ladder.prompt: Many students reverse the sign of the x-coordinate incorrectly. Remember that the bracket becomes zero at the turning point.

hint_ladder.title: The general pattern
hint_ladder.prompt: For y = (x - h)^2 + k, the turning point is (h, k). If you start from expanded form, complete the square first. Apply this pattern; do not copy an example.

expected_solution_steps.diagnostic_sentence: The stuck point is forming the correct square.
The stuck point is adjusting the constant after completing the square.
The stuck point is reading the turning point from completed-square form.

mark_scheme_notes: Award marks for completed-square form and correct turning point.
examiner_report_notes: Likely errors: wrong x-coordinate sign and constant adjustment errors.
metacognition_prompt: Before you start, what does completed-square form tell you about a graph?
